JetBlue.event: Weather shutdown day in New York: over 50% of JetBlue's New York flights cancelled on any day this winter
JetBlue.why_picked: JetBlue has been on my radar because of its recent organizational changes. It sits between a budget carrier and a major US airline, and as a mid-size airline concentrated in the Northeast, with about half its flights touching New York, it's hit harder by winter storms than bigger, more spread-out competitors.
key_facts: About half of JetBlue's daily flights start or end at a New York-area airport (FY2025 10-K).
Operating loss of $368M in 2025; load factor 82.4%, so little room to rebook stranded passengers.
Winter Storm Hernando, Feb 22-24, 2026: JetBlue cancelled up to 100% of its New York flights (BTS data).
Winter 2025-26 had two separate shutdowns of 2+ days (Jan 25-26 and Feb 22-24).
reasoning: Revenue hit: $9,062M revenue x 50% New York share / 365 = one shutdown day ($12.4M). Cross-checked with passengers x average fare ($11.4M).
Probability 50%: 10 winters of federal BTS flight data (2016-17 to 2025-26); 5 winters had at least one shutdown day. March 2020 excluded (COVID, not weather).
Limits: some revenue comes back through rebooking and higher fares on remaining seats; storm costs (de-icing, crews, hotels) push the other way.
Tradeoff: a 50% event makes the hedge pricey; covering only 2+ day storms (10%) is cheaper.

CoreWeave.event: H100 rental price index falls 25% or more over the next 12 months
CoreWeave.why_picked: Chose CoreWeave because it's an interesting company with secure revenue streams, which almost pushes it aside as a hedge candidate. But I wanted to see how it would turn out after looking at the other sources, and it turns out 98% of its revenue is locked into contracts, so the real question is what's left exposed.
key_facts: 98% of 2025 revenue came from take-or-pay committed contracts, about 5-year average duration (FY2025 10-K).
$60.7B of remaining performance obligations; Microsoft was 67% of 2025 revenue.
Interest expense of $1.2B in 2025; debt partly backed by GPUs.
H100 rental index: about $8/hr in early 2024, about $2.00 in Dec 2025, about $3.10 by Nov 2026.
reasoning: Exposure: only the ~2% on-demand slice (~$103M) moves with market GPU prices right away.
Revenue hit: ~$103M x a 25% price drop = $25.7M.
Probability 30%: history says ~65%, but those drops came from post-shortage normalization; prices have risen ~55% since Dec 2025 ($2.00 to ~$3.10) and capacity is sold out.
Bigger risks than price: customer concentration (Microsoft 67%) and GPU-backed debt.

Clearway.event: Low-wind year: wind output falls 5% below normal
Clearway.why_picked: Green economics is a key interest of mine, so I decided to go with a semi-popular player in the clean energy space with big reach in the US. Clearway also has thin margins and a heavy reliance on wind energy, so one calm year would majorly impact its profits.
key_facts: Wind is Clearway's largest technology: 3,708 net MW, about 38% of capacity (FY2025 10-K).
Operating income was only $160M in 2025 vs $387M of interest expense.
2023: lower-than-average wind production cut revenue by $43M (FY2023 10-K).
2021: $50M of settlements when wind farms couldn't deliver during the Texas freeze.
reasoning: Revenue hit: 10.5M wind MWh x ~$57.61/MWh x 5% shortfall = ~$30M. The price blends wind, solar and storage.
Why 5%: 2023 wind was ~4-5% below average and cost $43M, so 5% is realistic and possibly conservative.
Probability 20%: 1 low-wind year out of 5 (2021-2025); small sample.
Contracts lock in price but not volume: if the wind doesn't blow, Clearway isn't paid.

DC.event: Man of Tomorrow (July 9, 2027) opens below $100M domestic
DC.why_picked: Wanted to look at unstable markets, and film is one of them, with high volatility and a lot of unpredictable factors. So I chose a big studio that sits between blockbuster franchises and highly volatile box office conditions, which also ties into my Film Production minor.
key_facts: Paramount Skydance completed its ~$110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct 6, 2026.
Superman (2025) opened to $125M domestic, $354M domestic total, $619M worldwide.
Warner Bros. Studios segment revenue was $12.6B in 2025 (FY2025 10-K).
reasoning: Revenue hit: an $85M opening instead of $125M carries through the run (2.83x domestic, 1.75x worldwide) = ~$198M less box office; studio keeps ~50% = ~$99M.
Probability 25%: 5 of 10 superhero comps opened under $100M, but all 3 sequels to hits cleared $100M; adjusted up for DC brand risk after Supergirl.
Signal: every comp tracking above $100M opened above it, so buy the hedge before tracking slips (The Marvels fell from $75-80M to $46M).
Limits: excludes streaming and licensing, which also follow the opening.
